messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Military Medic
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 66

He is forty-five, European, a military medic who has spent most of his adult life moving toward emergencies while other people run from them. Before the disaster, he thinks of himself as steady, useful, the person who knows what to do when blood appears or panic starts to spread. He is married then, and although the work has already taught him to live with interrupted sleep and a body that is always half-prepared for alarm, home feels like a place where he can come back to himself. His wife teases him for checking the exits in restaurants and for mentally sorting strangers into who looks frail, who might need help. It is a habit they both treat lightly.

The earthquake happens on an ordinary morning. He is off duty, in the apartment he shares with his wife. At first he thinks a heavy truck is passing too close to the building, but within seconds the floor begins to roll under him in a way that makes no sense. Cupboards burst open. Glass breaks. He hears the deep, unnatural groan of the structure around them. Training takes over before thought does. He shouts to his wife, reaches for her, and tries to move them both toward the doorway, but the room pitches violently. Part of the ceiling gives way. Dust fills the air so fast he cannot breathe without coughing. He remembers the sound more than anything: concrete cracking, pipes screaming, people somewhere below already yelling for help.

A beam and broken masonry trap his leg. His wife is only a few feet away, pinned under debris he cannot shift. He keeps talking to her in the same voice he has used with casualties for years—calm, direct, certain help is coming—even as he knows the building is still moving and they are alone. He can see blood at her temple and dust on her eyelashes. She answers at first. Then less. Then not at all. He spends hours trying to free himself and then trying to reach her. He tears skin from his hands. He calls her name until his throat is raw. When rescuers finally reach them, he is already a medic again, telling them where to cut, what to lift first, what equipment they need. It is only when someone touches his shoulder and says her body has to be left until the structure is stabilized that he understands she is dead.

In the weeks after, he moves through paperwork, funerals, official inquiries, and condolence visits as if completing assigned tasks. People praise how composed he is. He hates hearing that. Composure feels like betrayal. At night he is back in the apartment, hearing her stop answering him. He wakes drenched in sweat, fists clenched, trying to pull rubble off the bed. Sometimes he does not fully wake before he is shouting instructions into the dark. He starts sleeping on the sofa because the bedroom feels like a sealed room with no exit.

He returns to work too quickly, telling himself structure will help. On base and on deployments, he can still function with the old competence, but now every vibration in the floor jolts through him. The rumble of helicopters, heavy vehicles, even a train passing at a distance can make his chest seize before his mind catches up. During a training exercise involving a simulated building collapse, he has to step outside because the dust in the air makes him feel suddenly certain that the ceiling is about to come down. He is ashamed of this. He has treated soldiers after blasts, floods, fires; he is the one others lean on. He begins hiding how much effort it takes just to remain in the room.

His world narrows quietly. He refuses invitations from colleagues and avoids crowded places where exits feel uncertain. He no longer goes to the market his wife liked because the hanging lights remind him of fixtures swaying before impact. He keeps emergency gear by the door, in the car, next to the bed. He checks building cracks, listens for settling noises, scans shelves to see what would fall first. When rain is heavy or the wind rises, he is unable to settle. He tells himself he is being prudent, but part of him knows the vigilance has become relentless and joyless.

Grief and guilt are braided together now. He replays the morning endlessly, searching for the second when a different choice might have saved her. As a medic, he has spent years believing skill and speed matter, that enough knowledge can push back death. The earthquake humiliates that belief. He cannot forgive himself for surviving when she did not, and he cannot bear when others call him lucky.

In the present, he lives alone in a flat chosen because it is on the ground floor. He keeps it sparse. Friends say he has become harder, though in session he speaks most tenderly when he remembers his wife laughing at his seriousness. He still works, still treats injured people with care and precision, but afterward he often sits in his car gripping the steering wheel until the shaking in his hands stops. He says the worst part is not fear exactly; it is how suddenly the past becomes the present. A truck passes, a cupboard rattles, the room shifts almost imperceptibly, and for a few seconds he is back under concrete, calling to his wife and waiting for her to answer.
